standard.title: Give and follow directions
standard.description: Give and follow directions to move people and objects to different locations within a space
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe position and location of themselves and objects within a familiar space (AC9MFSP02). They have not yet given or followed multi-step directional instructions, created algorithms for movement, or used ordinal and positional language to direct others.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students give and follow directions to move people and objects to different locations within a space.

nodes.label: Interpret and follow directions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can interpret and follow a sequence of directional instructions using forwards, backwards, left, right and straight ahead to reach a stated location.
nodes.minimum_width: Follow a three-step sequence of directions using at least two directional terms to reach a target location.
nodes.typical_width: Interpret and follow multi-step directions using forwards, backwards, straight ahead, left, right; understand that left/right are relative to the mover's orientation; follow directions given by a peer or teacher; reach target locations reliably.
wider: Follow directions that describe a familiar journey using landmark-based language from a First Nations perspective, recognising how directional language is shaped by relationship to Country/Place.
Program a floor robot (Bee-Bot or equivalent) by entering a direction sequence, testing it and debugging when the robot doesn't reach the target.

response_modes.reason: Left/right confusion is extremely common at Year 1 and requires targeted practice. Students need repeated experience with left/right from their own perspective — and from another person facing them — before they can reliably follow peer-given directions.

nodes.hinge_reason: Reliable left/right orientation is a prerequisite for Node 2 (giving directions) and Node 3 (creating algorithms) — students who confuse their own left/right give systematically incorrect directions and produce algorithms that fail when tested.
success_criteria: Follows a multi-step direction sequence correctly, reaching the target location.
Demonstrates correct understanding of left/right relative to own orientation.

nodes.label: Create and give directions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can create a sequence of directional instructions to move an object or person from one location to another, testing whether the instructions work.
nodes.minimum_width: Give a three-step direction sequence to move an object or peer to a new location; check whether the instructions were followed successfully.
nodes.typical_width: Create multi-step direction sequences using directional language; give instructions to a peer and observe whether the instructions are followed as intended; revise instructions if the target was not reached; use ordinal and positional language to describe positions within a line or space.
wider: Design a direction puzzle for a peer — writing the instructions on paper — and exchange puzzles, testing and giving feedback on precision.
Create an algorithm for a floor robot to reach a target, iterating the instruction sequence based on observed robot movement.

response_modes.reason: Writing directions from a giver's perspective requires spatial perspective-taking — imagining the path from the mover's point of view. Students who give ambiguous instructions (e.g. 'go forward a bit') need support in making the algorithm precise enough to be followed without interpretation.

success_criteria: Creates a direction sequence that successfully moves a person or object to the target location when followed exactly.
Revises the instructions when the target is not reached, identifying the specific instruction that caused the error.

nodes.label: Algorithms for movement
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can create a step-by-step algorithm of instructions to move an object or person through a space, recognising that each instruction must be precise and complete.
nodes.minimum_width: Create a movement algorithm of at least four steps; explain what an algorithm is (a set of instructions that must be followed exactly).
nodes.typical_width: Create and follow movement algorithms; recognise that ambiguous or imprecise instructions cause failure; refine algorithms based on testing; connect the robot role-play to the concept of a precise algorithmic instruction set.
wider: Program a digital floor robot using a sequence of coded direction instructions, comparing the precision required for digital instructions with the precision used in verbal instructions.

Create a direction narrative describing a journey across Country/Place, integrating landmark-based and compass-based directional language, and connecting to First Nations ways of describing movement through space.

response_modes.reason: Creating a complete, working movement algorithm requires students to coordinate spatial reasoning, directional language, sequence, and precision simultaneously. This is the integration node for the descriptor's full demand — and a genuine early encounter with algorithmic thinking.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The algorithmic movement context is the earliest encounter with computational thinking in the Mathematics curriculum. Students who understand that a movement algorithm must be precise and complete are building transferable reasoning about sequence and instruction that underpins Digital Technologies concepts.
success_criteria: Creates a movement algorithm that reaches the target when followed exactly.
Explains why each instruction in the algorithm must be precise.
